strengths: Novel and conceptually interesting idea: using the drift of linear-probe class weights in embedding space (rather than analyzing misclassified samples) to identify biases, offering a genuinely different angle than prior data-centric bias discovery methods (B2T, SpLiCE, Lg).
Provides a theoretical justification (cosine similarity bound, proven in appendix) motivating the proposed concept-ranking score.
Method is modality-agnostic and demonstrated on both vision (Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++) and text (CivilComments) tasks using different foundational models (CLIP, mGTE).
Shows worst-group accuracy improvements over zero-shot baseline and several bias-discovery baselines in a zero-shot prompting evaluation across four datasets.
Includes a useful qualitative comparison table (Table 4) contrasting fundamental design choices of prior bias-detection methods, clarifying positioning within related work.
Ablation study on ranking score formulation and top-q cutoff illustrates sensitivity of the pipeline to design choices.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage in the main quantitative table is highly incomplete (many '-' entries for B2T/SpLiCE/Lg on Nico++, CivilComments, and Waterbirds), making the claimed 'significant improvement over SoTA' only partially substantiated.

The core claim of discovering 'previously untapped biases' is validated almost entirely through subjective, author-annotated qualitative tables (color-coded red/green/blue judgments) rather than any objective/quantitative bias-identification metric (e.g., precision/recall against ground-truth spurious attributes), which is a weak form of evidence for the central contribution.

Average accuracy substantially drops for ConceptDrift-augmented prompting on some datasets (e.g., CivilComments average falls from 83.4% to 69.0%), indicating a worst-group vs. average accuracy trade-off that is not discussed or analyzed.

Hyperparameters such as top-q concepts appear tuned/chosen without a principled selection strategy, and the paper explicitly defers this to future work, weakening reproducibility and robustness claims.

The pipeline depends heavily on an image captioning model and heuristic keyword extraction (YAKE, WordNet filtering), introducing significant noise and bias into the discovered concepts that is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantified.
Nico++ experiments use a custom, small, non-standard subset (4 classes, 3 contexts) constructed by the authors, limiting comparability and generalizability of results.
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple-seed results are reported for the accuracy comparisons.

The theoretical bound (Eq. 2) is fairly loose and its practical necessity/impact on the final scoring heuristic is not empirically isolated (e.g., no comparison to simpler heuristics without this justification).

Minor clarity issues: inconsistent naming ('ConceptShift' vs 'ConceptDrift'), and the paper does not discuss computational cost or scalability of the pipeline (captioning + keyword extraction + ranking) relative to baselines.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually interesting idea: using the drift of linear probe weights from class-name text embeddings to identify biases directly imprinted in model decision boundaries, rather than relying solely on misclassified sample analysis (a genuine methodological departure from B2T and similar approaches).
The method is model/modality-agnostic in principle, and the authors demonstrate application to both vision (Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++) and text (CivilComments) settings using CLIP and mGTE.

A theoretical justification (Eq. 2, proven in the appendix) is provided connecting the cosine similarity of the class weight with a concept embedding to the similarity with samples containing that concept, giving some formal grounding to the ranking score.

The qualitative comparison table (Table 3) plus per-dataset appendix tables (Nico++, CivilComments) offer some interpretable insight into what kinds of biases are surfaced by the method versus prior work.
The ablation in Table 2 attempts to isolate the contribution of the scoring function and the top-q cutoff hyperparameter.
weaknesses: The core empirical validation (Table 1) is indirect: the method is evaluated only via its effect on zero-shot prompting accuracy after manually appending discovered bias words to prompts, not via any direct or quantitative validation that discovered concepts are actually causal/correlated biases (e.g., no precision/recall against known ground-truth biases, no human evaluation of concept correctness, no comparison against ground-truth bias annotations for Waterbirds/CelebA which are well known).

Baselines are incomplete and inconsistent across datasets: SpLiCE and Lg are only evaluated on CelebA, B2T only on Waterbirds/CelebA, leaving Nico++ and CivilComments compared only against a bare zero-shot baseline with no other SOTA competitor, undermining claims of being state-of-the-art across all four datasets.

Some reported results directly contradict the paper's narrative of clear superiority: on Waterbirds and CivilComments, ConceptDrift substantially reduces average accuracy (e.g., CivilComments avg drops from 83.4% to 69.0%) even though worst-group accuracy improves, suggesting the found 'biases' may not be reliable/general and the prompting protocol trades off overall performance heavily — this tradeoff is not adequately discussed or justified.

The improvement magnitude and choice of best template per class ('taking into account the score for the best one... max over templates') appears to constitute a form of test-set-driven prompt selection (oracle-like selection over templates), which is not clearly disentangled from the actual bias-ranking quality; this raises reproducibility and fairness-of-comparison concerns versus baselines if they don't use the same protocol.

No standard deviations, multiple seeds, or statistical significance are reported for any of the results, despite training a linear probe and using stochastic optimization (AdamW), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported numbers.

The keyword/concept extraction pipeline is a complex multi-stage heuristic (captioning model + YAKE n-grams + WordNet-based filtering + stopword removal) whose individual contributions and sensitivity to design choices are not ablated, despite being explicitly acknowledged as a major limitation; this makes it hard to know how much of the effect is due to the core 'weight drift' idea versus the concept-extraction engineering.

Table 4's comparison to related work is overly reductive (single-column high-level labels) and does not do justice to methodological differences or provide a rigorous head-to-head qualitative/quantitative comparison of bias-detection quality (precision of discovered biases, false positive rates, etc.).

The paper claims to 'pinpoint' true causal biases in model weights, but the theoretical bound (Eq. 2) only shows a necessary similarity relationship, not that a concept highly correlated with a class weight is actually a spurious/undesirable attribute vs. a legitimate discriminative feature; the dictionary-filtering step for distinguishing genuine biases from valid class-relevant concepts is described very briefly and seems to rely on brittle heuristics (WordNet hypernym/hyponym filtering), which is unlikely to generalize.

The paper is short and several important details are relegated to the appendix or omitted entirely (e.g., full details of the Nico++ custom dataset construction, statistical variance, how 'top-q' and threshold hyperparameters were tuned, whether the same hyperparameters were used across datasets), limiting reproducibility.

The writing has some clarity issues (e.g., 'ConceptShift' typo referring to the method as opposed to 'ConceptDrift', inconsistent capitalization) and the qualitative bias tables color-code good/bad/ambiguous concepts through subjective post-hoc human labeling, which is not a rigorous evaluation methodology.

Overall novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea of using embedding-space arithmetic to identify class-associated concepts is already present in prior work (Lg, SpLiCE); the main claimed novelty is initializing weights at the class-text embedding and tracking drift, which is a relatively small conceptual step over existing embedding-arithmetic bias-discovery methods.

strengths: The core idea of analyzing the drift of linear-probe classification weights (from the class name embedding toward spurious-attribute embeddings) is a genuinely novel angle for bias discovery, distinct from prior mistake-driven (B2T) or dictionary/embedding-arithmetic methods (SpLiCE, Lg) that operate purely on data.

The method is theoretically motivated: a clean derivation (Eq. 2, proved in the appendix) links high cosine similarity between a class weight and a concept embedding to high similarity between that weight and samples containing the concept, giving some justification for the proposed ranking score.
Modality-agnostic design, demonstrated on both vision (Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++) and text (CivilComments) tasks using different foundational backbones (CLIP, mGTE).
Worst-group accuracy improves over the zero-shot baseline and over reported prior bias-discovery baselines on all four datasets when the discovered bias words are used to augment prompts.

Qualitative analysis (Table 3, Fig. 2, Appendix tables) provides an interesting look into the concepts recovered, showing plausible new candidate biases (e.g., 'bamboo', 'snowy', 'smiles') not surfaced by prior methods, and a reasonable ablation on ranking-score variants and concept cut-off.
weaknesses: Substantial tradeoffs between worst-group and average accuracy are not adequately discussed, most notably on CivilComments where average accuracy drops sharply (83.4% -> 69.0%) even though worst-group accuracy improves; this raises concerns about whether the method is truly identifying useful biases or simply shifting the decision boundary in a way that trades off overall performance.

Baseline coverage is incomplete: B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg are only evaluated on a subset of datasets (many cells are '-'), making the comparison in Table 1 partial and harder to trust as a comprehensive demonstration of superiority.

The qualitative bias evaluation (Table 3, color-coded red/green/blue) is performed and labeled by the authors themselves with no independent human validation or quantitative agreement metric, which risks confirmation bias when claiming 'new' biases are correct.

The keyword-extraction pipeline (captioning model + YAKE n-grams + WordNet-based filtering) is a heuristic, multi-stage process with several hyperparameters (top-q, n-gram lengths, hypernym/hyponym filtering) that are not systematically ablated beyond top-q and the ranking score; robustness to these design choices, and to the specific captioning/embedding models used, is untested.

Only a single foundational model per modality is evaluated (CLIP ViT-L/14 for vision, mGTE for text); no experiments assess whether ConceptDrift generalizes across different backbone architectures or scales.

No variance/statistical significance is reported across runs, and results appear to come from single training runs, which is a concern given the relatively small worst-group accuracy differences in some datasets (e.g., CelebA 72.8 -> 75.6%).

The practical utility of the method is demonstrated only via zero-shot prompt augmentation; there is no experiment showing the identified biases can be used to actually retrain/mitigate bias in the fine-tuned classifier itself, limiting the demonstrated downstream impact.

The paper's claim of being 'first' to use a weight-space approach could be better contextualized against broader probing-classifier and interpretability literature that also studies classifier weight directions, which is not discussed in related work beyond the four directly compared bias-discovery methods.

strengths: Novel framing: shifts spurious correlation (SC) detection from error/data analysis to analyzing the drift of classifier weights during fine-tuning, addressing a real limitation of prior work (dependence on exhaustive validation counterexamples).
Multi-modal applicability, demonstrated on both image (Waterbirds, CelebA, ImageNet) and text (CivilComments) domains.

Extensive empirical validation: synthetic image generation via FLUX.1-dev used to probe discovered SCs, tested against a very large and diverse set of pretrained ImageNet classifiers (CNNs and transformers), showing consistent degradation when spurious concepts are introduced.

Reasonably thorough comparison against multiple relevant baselines (B2T, SpLiCE, Lg, GroupDRO, DrML discussion) across three tasks: zero-shot prompting, regularization in a fully-confounded setting, and qualitative concept discovery.
The 'fully spurious setup' experiment (Table 3) is a nice demonstration that WASP-derived concepts are useful even when GroupDRO-style methods fail completely due to absence of counterexamples.
Ablations on threshold selection and modality gap correction provide some insight into design choices.
Practically relevant finding: previously unreported learned SCs in a widely used, well-regarded CLIP/ImageNet classifier, which could have real-world implications for deployed models.
weaknesses: Methodologically, SCs are extracted from a linear probe trained on frozen foundation-model embeddings rather than from the actual full fine-tuned model referenced in the motivating example (Fig. 1); it's unclear how well conclusions transfer to genuinely fine-tuned end-to-end models versus reflecting biases already present in the foundation model's embedding space.

The pipeline chains several imperfect components (image captioning, YAKE keyword extraction, LLM-based filtering, WordNet post-processing), and error propagation/robustness of the overall SC discovery to failures in any of these stages is not analyzed.
The dynamic thresholding heuristic (Eq. 3) is intuitively motivated but lacks theoretical grounding or comparison to more principled alternatives beyond simple ablations.

Results are mixed in places (e.g., CelebA average accuracy decreases when using WASP-augmented zero-shot prompts relative to the plain zero-shot baseline, 85.7 vs 87.7), which slightly undercuts the claim of uniform improvement.

Validation of ImageNet-discovered SCs required manual curation and inspection of generated images, limiting the claimed scalability/full automation, and only a handful of qualitative cases were rigorously validated quantitatively (Table 1).

Synthetic images generated by FLUX.1-dev to validate spurious correlations may introduce their own generative artifacts/biases, which could confound the interpretation that the classifier is purely reacting to the intended spurious concept.
No statistical variance/multiple-seed reporting for the large-scale ImageNet model evaluation tables (Tables 2, 8–10), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported accuracy drops.
Limited comparison with some previously discussed related methods (e.g., DrML, CoBalT, Salient ImageNet) in the main quantitative tables, despite being discussed at length in related work.
Code is not yet available (placeholder in abstract), raising reproducibility concerns at review time.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely interesting and underexplored angle: inferring spurious correlations from the trained weights of a classification head rather than solely from validation errors or training-data statistics.
The method is applied across multiple modalities (image classification on Waterbirds/CelebA/ImageNet, text classification on CivilComments), showing some generality of the pipeline.

The ImageNet case study with synthetic image generation (FLUX.1-dev) and evaluation across roughly 90 pretrained architectures is an ambitious and fairly extensive empirical exercise that produces some compelling qualitative examples (e.g., the 'firefighter' concept fooling a fire-truck classifier).

The paper includes several types of downstream validation (regularization under fully spurious setups, spurious-aware zero-shot prompting, qualitative concept comparisons) rather than relying on a single evaluation protocol.
Ablations on thresholding strategy and modality-gap correction are provided, showing some methodological care.
weaknesses: The central claim that WASP detects concepts 'learned by the model' is undermined for the ImageNet experiments: the SC-identification pipeline trains a linear probe on frozen CLIP embeddings, yet the paper then asserts these same concepts are 'learned' by dozens of unrelated architectures (AlexNet, ResNet, ViT, etc.) that were never analyzed by WASP and were trained completely differently. This conflates dataset-level correlations with model-specific weight drift, contradicting the paper's own stated distinction from 'data-analysis' methods.

Quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly supportive: in Table 5, WASP's average accuracy is sometimes worse than the zero-shot baseline or competitors (e.g., CelebA average drops from 87.7% to 85.7%), and in Table 3 some worst-group gains (e.g., CelebA: 9.6→10.4) are small relative to the reported variance.

The synthetic-image validation in Table 1 covers only three hand-picked scenarios, which is a very small and seemingly cherry-picked sample relative to the claimed breadth of 'previously untapped' spurious correlations; no systematic/automated evaluation across a larger random sample of discovered SCs is provided.

The concept-discovery pipeline depends on a long chain of off-the-shelf components (GIT captioning, YAKE keyword extraction, LLM-based filtering, WordNet post-processing) with no ablation or error analysis of how noise/errors at each stage propagate into the final SC rankings, raising reproducibility and reliability concerns.

There is no human evaluation or inter-annotator validation of whether the concepts flagged as 'spurious' are truly causally unrelated to the class versus legitimate correlated features; the paper relies entirely on automatic filtering and its own scoring heuristic.

The dynamic-thresholding heuristic (Eq. 3) is presented without strong theoretical justification, and the ablation only compares against two naive fixed-cutoff baselines, leaving open whether the specific curve-distance heuristic is well-founded or simply post-hoc tuned to the datasets studied.

The fairness disclaimer regarding CivilComments (explicitly stating the method is not designed to address fairness) sits uneasily with the fact that the discovered 'SCs' include racially/religiously loaded terms; the implications of surfacing such correlations without deeper analysis are not adequately discussed.
Code is not available at submission time (promised only upon acceptance), limiting independent verification of the fairly complex pipeline.
Comparisons to baselines such as Lg are partly based on the authors' own re-implementation in some settings (e.g., Table 3), raising some concern about the fairness of the comparison.

strengths: Genuinely novel angle on spurious correlation detection: analyzing weight-space drift of a trained linear layer relative to its zero-shot initialization, rather than relying on validation errors or frozen data statistics, which addresses a real limitation of prior work (B2T, SpLiCE, LG) that cannot surface SCs absent from counterexamples.

Demonstrated applicability across modalities (image: Waterbirds/CelebA/ImageNet; text: CivilComments) with a common underlying formulation, suggesting the approach is not narrowly tailored to a single domain.

Strong and creative validation strategy: generating synthetic images (via FLUX.1-dev) that isolate a discovered spurious concept and showing dramatic drops in correct-class softmax/accuracy and corresponding increases in the induced (unillustrated) class, tested extensively across dozens of ImageNet-1k architectures in the appendix, lending robustness to the central claim.

Practical downstream utility is shown in two separate ways: (1) an SC-based regularization loss that outperforms GroupDRO and ERM baselines in a fully spurious (no-counterexample) setup, and (2) SC-aware zero-shot prompting that improves worst-group accuracy over competing SC-discovery methods across all three benchmark datasets.

Reasonable ablations on the dynamic thresholding mechanism and the text-image modality gap, and qualitative comparisons (Table 4) showing WASP surfaces additional/different concepts than prior methods.
Transparent, fully automated pipeline (no manual concept curation) that could scale to large label spaces such as ImageNet-1k, together with an explicit algorithm box for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The pipeline for candidate concept generation (captioning model + YAKE keyword extraction + LLM/WordNet filtering) is a chain of heuristic components whose individual error/coverage limitations are not analyzed; failures here would silently bound what SCs WASP can discover, but this is not stress-tested.

No human evaluation or inter-annotator validation of whether the concepts flagged as SCs are actually causally unrelated to the class versus benign co-occurring features; the qualitative tables (e.g., Table 4) rely on the authors' own subjective red/blue labeling.

Quantitative validation of ImageNet SCs (Sec 5.1/Table 1) is limited to only three hand-picked scenarios, and the authors admit they had to manually vet generated images for correctness, raising concerns about selection bias in which SCs are showcased versus the full set the method outputs.

Synthetic-image-based validation could itself be confounded by generative model artifacts/biases (FLUX.1-dev) that correlate with the induced classes for reasons unrelated to the tested SC, and this alternative explanation is not fully ruled out.

Mixed results in Table 5: while worst-group accuracy improves with WASP-augmented zero-shot prompts, average accuracy sometimes decreases relative to the vanilla zero-shot baseline (e.g., CelebA avg. 85.7 vs. 87.7), which is not discussed or explained in the text.
The dynamic thresholding heuristic (Eq. 3) for selecting the SC cut-off is intuitively motivated but lacks theoretical grounding or sensitivity analysis beyond a small ablation table.

The method operates on a linear probe over frozen foundation-model embeddings rather than the fully fine-tuned model's actual weights in deployment, which may only approximate the SCs learned by a genuinely fine-tuned end-to-end model.

Fairness implications are raised (CivilComments touches on protected attributes) but are largely deferred to future work with only a brief disclaimer, despite the method being directly relevant to bias/fairness auditing use cases.

No direct quantitative comparison against subpopulation-shift-specific baselines (CoBalT, XRM, JTT, etc.) on the same metrics, only a qualitative discussion, making it harder to gauge relative standing against that closely related line of work.
